title: State Homekey grants per home: San Francisco against the rest of California
question: How much did the State award per home for San Francisco’s Homekey projects, round by round, compared with projects elsewhere in California?
finding: San Francisco has 11 of the 318 Homekey awards that list homes: $313,698,953 for 1,080 homes, $290,462 a home against $241,070 for the rest of the State. Homekey Round 1: the middle San Francisco award was $214,672 a home against $127,907 elsewhere (2 of 94 awards). Homekey Round 2: the middle San Francisco award was $331,337 a home against $285,129 elsewhere (4 of 116 awards). Homekey Round 3: the middle San Francisco award was $307,376 a home against $286,992 elsewhere (2 of 51 awards). Homekey+: the middle San Francisco award was $326,255 a home against $361,989 elsewhere (3 of 57 awards). The highest against its round is Homekey 2 (440 Geary St) at $223,077 a home, 1.74 times the middle award elsewhere and number 2 of 94.
how: Every award in the State housing department’s Homekey lists (Rounds 1, 2 and 3 and Homekey+), as collected in one table by the download step; the total award divided by the total homes listed. Each San Francisco award is set against the middle award per home of all other awards in the same round and ranked within the round (1 is the highest per home). By city, San Francisco ranks 2 of 61 in Homekey Round 1; 17 of 76 in Homekey Round 2; 15 of 36 in Homekey Round 3; 23 of 37 in Homekey+ on award per home.
limits: An award per home is what the State granted, not what a building cost: the City or a nonprofit pays the rest, and awards mix purchase money with operating subsidy in different proportions. Rounds had different rules and caps, land and buildings cost more in San Francisco than in most of the State, and a project that builds new or converts offices is not the same good as a motel purchase. Project names and uses in three of the lists were read from the layout of a PDF and can be misaligned; the award and unit numbers were checked against the printed totals. This screen uses no assessor data; for the buildings themselves, the roll’s limits apply: it records no price, only a sale date and assessed values, and the recorded deed and transfer-tax declaration would settle what was paid.
